overview.title: 📖 Overview: What Was Lost, What Was Restored, and a New Mishna
overview.subtitle: Temurah 16a–16b
overview.hebrewSource: אַרְבָּעָה נִתְּנוּ לָהֶן, וְהֶעֱמִידוּם עַל חָמֵשׁ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues its meditation on forgotten Torah: three thousand halakhot, and later seventeen hundred a fortiori inferences and verbal analogies, were lost during the mourning for Moses — the latter restored only through Otniel ben Kenaz's brilliant reasoning, celebrated in the story of his marriage to Caleb's daughter Achsah. The Gemara then returns to halakha, working out exactly how Rabbi Shimon's five 'sin offerings left to die' were transmitted at Sinai — a dispute between Reish Lakish (four given directly, a fifth added by analogy) and Rabbi Natan (only one given directly, four added by analogy) — and why three of the five could never apply to a communal offering to begin with. The daf closes by opening a new mishna: the comparative stringencies between consecrated animals and their substitutes, in both directions.

slides.title: 😢 Grief, Forgetting, and a Refusal to Ask Heaven
slides.subtitle: Joshua, then Samuel, decline heavenly guidance to recover lost halakhot

steps.content: 1️⃣ 3,000 halakhot were forgotten during the mourning period for Moses. The people ask Joshua to seek heavenly guidance to recover them
2️⃣ Joshua refuses: 'לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִיא' — 'It is not in Heaven' (Deut. 30:12) — halakha is no longer determined by prophecy

3️⃣ Later, before his own death, Moses offers to resolve Joshua's doubts — but Joshua, having 'never left the tent,' says he has none, and immediately loses 300 halakhot and gains 700 new uncertainties
4️⃣ God tells Joshua the halakhot cannot be restored — instead, distract the people with war (the invasion of Canaan) so they forget their anger at him

callout.label: Later loss:
callout.text: A further 1,700 a fortiori inferences (kal vachomer), verbal analogies (gezeirot shavot), and scribal fine points were also forgotten during Moses' mourning.

slides.title: 💡 Otniel ben Kenaz Recovers What Was Lost
slides.subtitle: Sharp reasoning succeeds where mourning could not
slides.hebrewSource: וַיִּלְכְּדָהּ עׇתְנִיאֵל בֶּן קְנַז... וַיִּתֶּן לוֹ אֶת עַכְסָה בִתּוֹ לְאִשָּׁה
slides.label: The story:
slides.text: Rabbi Abbahu teaches that Otniel ben Kenaz restored the 1,700 forgotten teachings through sheer intellectual sharpness (פִּלְפּוּלוֹ), reading the conquest of 'Kiryat Sefer' — 'the city of the book' — as a metaphor for reclaiming lost Torah. Caleb rewarded him with his daughter Achsah's hand. The Gemara then unpacks Achsah's own request for 'upper and lower springs' (Joshua 15:19): she asks her father not for wealth but recognizes her husband, devoted purely to Torah, cannot provide it — so Caleb gives fertile fields instead. Otniel/Jabez's prayer (I Chronicles 4:10) is read by Rabbi Natan as a plea for Torah, students, retained learning, worthy friends, and freedom from the evil inclination — and by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as a more literal prayer for health, children, and livelihood.

slides.title: 🔢 How Many 'Dying' Sin Offerings Came From Sinai?
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Natan disagree on the transmission

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: FOUR sin-offering cases were given directly at Sinai as 'left to die.' A fifth was also meant to be included, but since the Sages forgot WHICH one, they applied 'dies' to all five, for safety.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Natan
lines.text: No — only ONE case was given directly as 'dies.' The other four were meant to merely GRAZE, but since it was forgotten which was which, all five were treated as dying.

lines.speaker: Shared logic
lines.text: Either way: since the directly-given cases include ones that structurally CANNOT apply to a community (offspring, temurah, owner-death), the transmission must have been about individual offerings only.

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: This is how Rabbi Shimon justifies applying the rule to the two ambiguous cases (atonement-by-replacement, year passed) as individual-only too — 'learn the unspecified from the specified.'

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: Both opinions reach the same halakhic outcome by different routes — but disagree sharply on how much was originally clear versus reconstructed.

slides.title: 📋 Why Three of Rabbi Shimon's Five Can't Be Communal
slides.subtitle: Structural impossibilities vs. genuinely ambiguous cases
headers: Why it can't (or might) apply to a community
rows: Communities never bring FEMALE sin offerings — so there's no communal offspring case at all
A community cannot perform temurah in the first place
'A community does not die' (established earlier, daf 15)
No structural block — genuinely ambiguous, resolved by analogy to the other three
Also ambiguous — resolved the same way

callout.label: The logical move:
callout.text: Since three cases are unambiguously individual-only, and all five were transmitted together as one halakhic unit, the remaining two must follow the same pattern.

slides.title: ⚖️ New Mishna: Kodashim vs. Temurah — Mutual Stringencies
slides.subtitle: Each side is stricter than the other in different ways

boxes.title: Consecrated Animals Stricter
items: Consecrated animals generate a substitute; a substitute cannot generate another
Community/partners CAN consecrate animals, but CANNOT perform temurah on them
One can consecrate fetuses and limbs directly, but cannot substitute for them

boxes.title: Temurah Stricter
items: A non-sacred animal with a PERMANENT blemish, substituted for an unblemished offering, receives full inherent sanctity
Ordinary consecration cannot confer that level of sanctity on a permanently blemished animal
(Continues onto the next daf with further stringencies)

callout.label: The pattern for the chapter ahead:
callout.text: Temurah and ordinary consecration aren't simply 'stricter' or 'more lenient' than each other across the board — each has its own unique severities the other lacks.

summary.principle: Even fundamental halakhot were forgotten and only partly reconstructed after Moses' death, and this same 'unspecified from the specified' method explains why all five of Rabbi Shimon's disqualified sin offerings are individual-only — setting up a new mishna on the mutual stringencies between consecration and temurah.

flowSteps.content: 😢 3,000 halakhot, then 1,700 inferences, forgotten in Moses' mourning — recovery from Heaven refused
💡 Otniel ben Kenaz restores them through sharp reasoning; wins Achsah as his reward

columns.content: 🔢 Reish Lakish (4 given) vs. R' Natan (1 given) — same conclusion, different routes
📋 3 of 5 dying sin offerings structurally can't be communal; 2 inferred by analogy

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: learn the unspecified case from the specified ones when they were transmitted as one halakhic unit

quiz.q: How did Joshua respond when the Jewish people asked him to seek heavenly guidance to recover the 3,000 forgotten halakhot?
o: He immediately asked God and received the answers
He refused, citing 'It is not in Heaven' (Deut. 30:12) — halakha is no longer determined by prophecy
He asked Samuel to do it instead
He said the halakhot were never really lost
quiz.e: Joshua invoked the principle that Torah law, once given at Sinai, is decided by the Sages of each generation, not by renewed prophecy — 'לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִיא.'

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Abbahu, how did Otniel ben Kenaz restore the 1,700 forgotten a fortiori inferences and verbal analogies?
o: Through a new prophecy
Through his sharp reasoning and intellectual acumen (פִּלְפּוּלוֹ), metaphorically described as conquering 'Kiryat Sefer'
By asking Moses directly
By finding a hidden scroll
quiz.e: Rabbi Abbahu explains that Otniel's conquest of Kiryat Sefer ('the city of the book') is a metaphor for recovering the lost teachings purely through his own sharp analytical reasoning.

quiz.q: According to Reish Lakish, how many of Rabbi Shimon's five 'dying' sin offering cases were directly transmitted at Sinai, and what happened to the rest?
o: All five were directly transmitted
Four were directly transmitted; since it was forgotten which fifth case belonged, all five were treated as dying
None were transmitted; all five are pure rabbinic enactments
Only two were transmitted
quiz.e: Reish Lakish holds that four cases were given directly as 'dies' at Sinai, and since the Sages forgot which fifth case also belonged, they applied the stringent 'dies' ruling to all five as a precaution.

quiz.q: Why can a sin offering's OFFSPRING never be a communal case, according to the Gemara?
o: Communities never bring sin offerings at all
Communities never bring FEMALE sin offerings, and only a female sin offering could give birth
Offspring are always sacrificed immediately
There is no reason given
quiz.e: Since communal sin offerings are always male (per the earlier mishna on daf 14), there is no scenario of a communal female sin offering giving birth, making the 'offspring' case structurally impossible for a community.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna opening at the end of the daf, in what way are consecrated animals (kodashim) stricter than a substitute (temurah)?
o: Consecrated animals can never be sacrificed
Consecrated animals generate a substitute, while a substitute cannot itself generate a further substitute; also, one can consecrate fetuses/limbs directly but not substitute for them
Consecrated animals are always communal
There is no such distinction
quiz.e: The mishna lists several ways ordinary consecration is more powerful: it can generate a substitute (unlike a substitute itself), and it can apply directly to fetuses and limbs, even though substitution cannot reach those cases.
